title: High School Profit and the District
bigQuestion: Is a Friday-night game mainly a public ritual or a source of money, and should a school district show the public its numbers?

story.title: A Check and an Agenda
story.kicker: On the same autumn evening, a booster club hands over a check and a school board posts a budget item.
paragraphs: It is a Friday in October in a small Illinois town. At four o'clock, the booster club president drops an envelope at the high school office. Inside is a check for new scoreboard lights. The booster club is its own nonprofit group, run by parents. It raised the money selling concessions and holding a raffle.

Two days earlier, the district office posted an agenda for Monday's school board meeting. Illinois law requires that agenda to go up at least 48 hours before a regular meeting. Item seven reads: "Accept donation from Athletic Boosters." Item nine reads: "Approve fall athletic budget."

At seven o'clock, the stadium lights come on. The band plays the national anthem. Students in the stands wear school colors. Adults pay at the gate, and volunteers count the cash at halftime. The police officer at the gate is paid from a different budget line than the ticket sellers.

On Monday night, a parent stands at the public comment microphone. She asks a plain question: "Did Friday's game make money or lose money?" The superintendent says the answer depends on which costs you count. The board members look at each other. No one has a single number ready.

The question is not new. American schools have argued about the money around games for more than a century. The answer depends on history: who took control of school sport, what the law says about public records, and why a game night means more to a town than a ticket count.
story.think: What costs of a Friday game might not appear in the athletic budget at all?

lessons.title: When Students Ran the Teams
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1800s students often ran their own school teams, and adults took control to deal with money, eligibility and disorder.
reading: In the late 1800s, many American high school teams were run by students. Students raised money, set schedules and sometimes hired coaches. Games were often played against colleges, clubs or town teams. Rules about who could play were loose or missing.

Problems followed. Some teams used *ringers*, players who were not really students at the school. Some players were much older than their classmates. Gate money went into the hands of whoever ran the team. School leaders and town newspapers began to complain.

Educators answered by bringing sport under adult control. In New York City, Luther Halsey Gulick helped found the Public Schools Athletic League in 1903. It set standards for play among the city's public schools. Across the country, principals and teachers took charge of *eligibility*, meaning the rules about who may play. Once schools ran sport, school officials also answered for its money.

words.d: a player brought in who is not truly eligible, such as a non-student on a school team
the rules about who may play, such as age, enrollment and grades
the New York City league for public schools, founded in 1903

look.title: A Team Treasurer, Around 1895
look.text: Picture a high school team around 1895. A student treasurer keeps the gate money in a tin box. He pays for a train trip to a game with a town club. No teacher checks the box or the roster. Two players on the roster no longer attend the school.
look.prompt: What two problems in this scene would lead school leaders to take control of the team?

check.q: What was a ringer on an early school team?
choices: a player who was not truly eligible, such as a non-student
check.why: A ringer was a player brought in who was not really eligible to play for the school.

check.q: Who helped found New York's Public Schools Athletic League in 1903?
check.why: Luther Halsey Gulick helped found the Public Schools Athletic League in 1903.

check.q: Why did school control of sport also bring the money under school officials?
choices: Students were banned from attending games
The federal government took the gate money
Once schools ran sport, officials answered for its funds
check.why: When principals and teachers took charge of teams, they also became responsible for the money.

lessons.title: A Private Body, a Public Role
lessons.mainIdea: In 2001 the Supreme Court ruled that a state high school athletic association can be treated as a part of government under the Constitution.
reading: State athletic associations are usually private nonprofit groups. Yet their members are mostly public schools, and their leaders are often public school officials. That raises a question. When an association makes a rule, is it a private club acting, or is it the government?

In Brentwood Academy v. Tennessee Secondary School Athletic Association, decided in 2001, the Supreme Court answered. Brentwood Academy, a private school, had been penalized for recruiting rules violations. It sued. The Court ruled 5 to 4 that the Tennessee association was a *state actor*, meaning its actions count as government action.

The ruling matters because the Constitution limits government, not private clubs. A state actor must respect rights such as free speech and *due process*, which means fair procedures before a penalty. An association like the IHSA shapes public school life. Courts can review its rules much as they review the rules of a school district.

words.d: a person or group whose actions count as government action under the Constitution
fair procedures the government must follow before it takes away a right or gives a penalty
an organization that uses its income for its purpose instead of paying owners

look.title: Who Is Acting?
look.text: An association's board is made up of principals from public schools. It meets on school time. Its money comes mostly from tickets to state tournaments held for public schools. It votes to suspend a school's team for a season.
look.prompt: Using the words state actor, explain why a court might treat this vote as government action.

check.q: What did the Court decide in Brentwood Academy (2001)?
choices: Private schools cannot join athletic associations
Recruiting is protected by the Constitution
The Tennessee association was a state actor
check.why: The Court ruled 5 to 4 that the Tennessee association's actions counted as government action.

check.q: What is due process?
choices: a way to count gate money
the order of games in a tournament
fair procedures before the government takes away a right or gives a penalty
check.why: Due process means fair procedures, which a state actor must follow.

check.q: Why does being a state actor matter?
choices: The Constitution limits government action, so the group must respect rights
It makes the group a for-profit business
It lets the group ignore courts
It means the group writes federal law
check.why: The Constitution binds government, so a state actor must respect rights like free speech and due process.

lessons.title: Homecoming and a Town's Team
lessons.mainIdea: Homecoming and Friday-night football tie a school to its whole town, as both local traditions and later studies show.
reading: *Homecoming* is a yearly celebration that invites graduates back to their school, often built around a football game. Several schools claim to have held the first one. Baylor University points to 1909. The University of Illinois held a large homecoming in 1910. The University of Missouri claims 1911. Historians treat the first-ever claim as unsettled, but all three dates fall in the same few years.

High schools took up homecoming across the country. It brought parades, dances and alumni to the Friday game. Many schools also crowned a homecoming court chosen by student vote. The game became a meeting place for people who no longer had children in school. A team could stand for a whole town's identity.

In 1990 journalist H. G. Bissinger published Friday Night Lights: A Town, a Team, and a Dream. He spent the 1988 season with Permian High School in Odessa, Texas. His book described how much the town's hopes rested on teenage players. It also raised hard questions about school priorities, money and race in a football town.

words.d: a yearly celebration that invites graduates back to their school, often around a football game
graduates of a school
a custom a community repeats and passes down over years

look.title: Three Homecoming Claims
look.cite: Homecoming histories of Baylor University, the University of Illinois and the University of Missouri
look.prompt: The claims differ by only two years. Why might it be hard to prove which school was first?

check.q: Which Illinois school held a large homecoming in 1910?
check.why: The University of Illinois held its homecoming in 1910; Baylor claims 1909 and Missouri 1911.

check.q: What did H. G. Bissinger's 1990 book describe?
choices: the 1988 season of Permian High School in Odessa, Texas
check.why: Friday Night Lights followed Permian High School's 1988 season and the town's hopes around it.

check.q: How do historians treat the claims to the first homecoming?
check.why: Several schools claim the first homecoming, and historians treat the question as unsettled.

lessons.title: A Halftime Figure Retired
lessons.mainIdea: The University of Illinois retired its Chief Illiniwek halftime performance in 2007, after years of protest and a 2005 NCAA policy.
reading: A *mascot* is a figure, animal or symbol that stands for a team. Mascots are part of the civic ritual of a game. They appear at halftime, on uniforms and in school songs. Because they stand for a whole community, arguments about them often reach school boards and trustees.

In 1926 a University of Illinois student performed at a football halftime dressed as an American Indian chief. The figure, called Chief Illiniwek, appeared at games for about eighty years. Students played the role, and the figure danced with the marching band at halftime. Beginning in 1989, Charlene Teters, a Spokane graduate student at the university, led public protests against it. Native American groups and many faculty members called it a *stereotype*, an oversimplified picture of a group of people.

In August 2005 the NCAA adopted a policy barring schools with Native American mascots or imagery it judged hostile or abusive from hosting its postseason events. Illinois was on the list. The last official performance came on February 21, 2007, at a men's basketball game. Since then, many school boards across the country have held public votes on Native American team names and mascots.

words.d: a figure, animal or symbol that stands for a team
an oversimplified picture of a group of people
the board that governs a public university, like a school board for a district

look.title: A Board Agenda Item
look.text: A high school board posts an agenda item: "Discussion of team name and mascot." Alumni sign up to speak for keeping the name, citing decades of tradition. Native American families from the region sign up to speak for changing it, saying it misrepresents their people. The board must vote in open session.
look.prompt: Why is a mascot a question for a public board, and not only for the team?

check.q: When did the Chief Illiniwek halftime performance begin?
check.why: A University of Illinois student first performed as Chief Illiniwek at a football halftime in 1926.

check.q: Who began leading public protests against the figure in 1989?
check.why: Charlene Teters, a Spokane graduate student at Illinois, led protests beginning in 1989.

check.q: What did the NCAA's 2005 policy do?
choices: It required every school to use an animal mascot
It barred schools with Native American imagery it judged hostile or abusive from hosting postseason events
It paid schools to keep their mascots
check.why: The August 2005 policy kept listed schools, including Illinois, from hosting NCAA postseason events.

lessons.title: Prayer Over the Loudspeaker
lessons.mainIdea: In 2000 the Supreme Court ruled that a school-sponsored prayer over the loudspeaker before public high school games violated the First Amendment.
reading: A public school game is a school event, so the First Amendment applies. The First Amendment forbids government from *establishing* a religion. It also protects free speech and the free exercise of religion. Courts have had to decide how those rules fit a Friday-night crowd.

In Santa Fe Independent School District v. Doe (2000), a Texas district let an elected student give a prayer over the public-address system before home football games. The Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that this violated the *Establishment Clause*. The Court said the prayer was school-sponsored, because it used school property, a school system and a school event.

The Santa Fe ruling built on an earlier case. In Lee v. Weisman (1992), the Court had ruled 5 to 4 that a public middle school could not invite a clergy member to lead a prayer at its graduation. Both cases asked whether a school event made a prayer the school's own. In 2022 the Court drew a different line for an individual, ruling in Kennedy v. Bremerton School District that a coach's personal prayer after games was protected.

words.d: the part of the U.S. Constitution protecting religion, speech, press, assembly and petition
the First Amendment rule that government may not establish or sponsor a religion
done or supported by the school itself, not only by an individual

look.title: A Graduation and a Kickoff
look.text: Case A, 1992: a middle school principal invites a rabbi to give a prayer at graduation. Case B, 2000: students vote to choose one student, who gives a prayer over the stadium loudspeaker before each home game. In both cases the Court ruled against the school.
look.prompt: The school chose the speaker in Case A but students chose in Case B. Why did the Court still treat Case B as school-sponsored?

check.q: What did the Court decide in Santa Fe v. Doe (2000)?
choices: A student-led loudspeaker prayer before games was school-sponsored and not allowed
check.why: The Court ruled 6 to 3 that the pregame prayer violated the Establishment Clause.

check.q: What does the Establishment Clause forbid?
choices: government establishing or sponsoring a religion
all prayer by anyone at any game
the playing of the national anthem
check.why: The Establishment Clause keeps government from sponsoring a religion.

check.q: What did the Court decide in Lee v. Weisman (1992)?
choices: A coach may pray at midfield
A school could not invite clergy to lead a prayer at graduation
check.why: In Lee v. Weisman the Court ruled 5 to 4 against a clergy-led prayer at a public school graduation.

lessons.title: Meetings the Public Can Watch
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois' Open Meetings Act requires school boards to decide budgets, including athletic spending, in meetings the public can attend.
reading: An elected school board runs each Illinois public school district. Board members vote on budgets, contracts and gifts, including money for sports. Illinois passed its *Open Meetings Act* in 1957. It says public bodies must do their business in the open.

Under the act, a board must post an *agenda*, a list of items to be discussed, at least 48 hours before a regular meeting. Final votes must be taken in open session. The act also lets members of the public address the board, under rules the board sets. Closed sessions are allowed only for listed reasons, such as some personnel matters.

In 2010 Illinois created a Public Access Counselor in the Attorney General's office. The counselor reviews complaints that a public body broke the Open Meetings Act or the Freedom of Information Act. A parent who thinks a board voted on athletic spending in secret can ask the counselor to review it.

words.d: the 1957 Illinois law requiring public bodies to meet and vote in the open
a list of items a public body will discuss at a meeting
the elected body that governs a public school district
an office in the Illinois Attorney General's office, created in 2010, that reviews open-government complaints

look.title: An Agenda Posted Late
look.text: A board posts its agenda on Sunday at noon for a regular Monday meeting at seven o'clock. One item is a $40,000 contract for new stadium seating. A parent notices the posting time and writes to the state.
look.prompt: Using the 48-hour rule, explain the parent's complaint and which office could review it.

check.q: When did Illinois pass its Open Meetings Act?
check.why: Illinois passed the Open Meetings Act in 1957; the Public Access Counselor was created in 2010.

check.q: How far ahead must a board post the agenda for a regular meeting?
check.why: The Open Meetings Act requires the agenda to be posted at least 48 hours before a regular meeting.

check.q: What does the Public Access Counselor do?
choices: reviews complaints about open meetings and public records
check.why: The counselor, in the Attorney General's office, reviews complaints under the Open Meetings Act and FOIA.

lessons.title: Asking for the Records
lessons.mainIdea: Freedom of information laws let anyone ask a public school district for its records, including athletic budgets and gate receipts.
reading: The federal *Freedom of Information Act*, or FOIA, was signed in 1966. It covers federal agencies, not school districts. Illinois passed its own Freedom of Information Act in 1984. Illinois rewrote that law in a major way, effective January 1, 2010. The rewritten law says public records are presumed open unless a listed exception applies.

A *public record* is a document a public body creates or keeps about its business. For a school district, that includes budgets, contracts, invoices and many financial reports. Records of *gate receipts*, the money taken in at ticket sales, are kept by the district when the district runs the gate. Some records, such as private student information, are protected.

The rewritten law set time limits. A public body generally has five business days to respond, and it may extend that once for five more. People often use FOIA requests to learn what a stadium project cost or how much a district paid game officials. Reporters in Illinois have used the law to write about school spending.

words.d: a law that lets people request records from government bodies; Illinois passed its own in 1984
a document a public body creates or keeps about its business
the money taken in from ticket sales at a game

look.title: Three Requests
look.text: Request 1 asks for the total ticket sales at last fall's home games. Request 2 asks for the invoice from the company that installed the scoreboard. Request 3 asks for the grades of every player on the team.
look.prompt: Which two requests ask for public records a district would likely release, and which one asks for protected student information?

check.q: When was the Illinois Freedom of Information Act first passed?
check.why: Illinois passed its FOIA in 1984; the federal FOIA dates from 1966 and does not cover school districts.

check.q: What are gate receipts?
choices: the money taken in from ticket sales at a game
the list of players on a roster
check.why: Gate receipts are ticket-sale money, which a district records when it runs the gate.

check.q: Under the rewritten Illinois FOIA, how are public records treated?
choices: They are secret unless a judge orders release
They are presumed open unless an exception applies
They must be destroyed after one year
check.why: The 2010 rewrite presumes public records are open unless a listed exception applies.

lessons.title: Booster Clubs and Equal Treatment
lessons.mainIdea: Booster clubs are separate groups that raise money for teams, and Title IX still requires schools to treat boys' and girls' programs equally overall.
reading: A *booster club* is a group, usually of parents and fans, that raises money for a school team or activity. Many booster clubs are organized as separate nonprofit corporations. Their money often pays for equipment, travel, banquets and facility upgrades. Because they are separate, their own books are not always part of the district's budget.

Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 bans sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money. School sports count. Federal rules require schools to provide equal treatment to boys' and girls' athletic programs overall, in areas such as equipment, facilities, scheduling and travel.

The U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights looks at what athletes actually receive. It does not matter whether the benefit came from the district or from boosters. If one team's boosters buy far better gear or facilities, the school may have to make up the difference for the other sex's teams. This is one reason districts track booster gifts at board meetings.

words.d: a group, usually of parents and fans, that raises money for a school team or activity
the 1972 federal law banning sex discrimination in federally funded education programs, including sports
the U.S. Department of Education office that enforces Title IX

look.title: Two Locker Rooms
look.text: A boys' team's booster club pays to remodel its locker room with new lockers and a video screen. The girls' teams in the same season still use an older locker room with no upgrades. The district paid for neither project. A parent files a complaint with the Office for Civil Rights.
look.prompt: Why could the school, and not only the booster club, be responsible for the difference?

check.q: What is a booster club?
choices: a group of parents and fans that raises money for a team
check.why: A booster club raises money for a team and is often a separate nonprofit.

check.q: Under Title IX, why can booster gifts matter?
choices: The law looks at the benefits athletes receive, whatever the source
Boosters must pay federal taxes on gifts
Boosters vote on the IHSA bylaws
Title IX applies only to colleges
check.why: The Office for Civil Rights looks at what athletes receive, so booster-funded benefits count.

check.q: When was Title IX passed?
check.why: Congress passed Title IX in 1972 as part of a larger education law.

lessons.title: What Counts as a Cost
lessons.mainIdea: Whether a game makes a profit depends on which costs a district counts, because many game costs sit in different budget lines.
reading: *Profit* is the money left after costs are subtracted from income. For a Friday game, income may include tickets, concessions, programs and sponsor signs. Costs may include game officials, security, ticket takers, bus trips and electricity for the lights. A district may also count coaching stipends, equipment and field upkeep.

School budgets are split into *funds*, which are separate accounts for separate purposes. Illinois districts keep an education fund, an operations and maintenance fund and a transportation fund, among others. A stadium's electricity may be paid from one fund and the visiting team's bus from another. The ticket money may sit in a student activity account.

Illinois school law requires each district to publish a yearly report of its finances, called the Statement of Affairs. Districts also file an Annual Financial Report with the Illinois State Board of Education. Neither report is built to show one game's profit. To answer that question, someone must choose which costs belong to the game and add them up.

words.d: the money left after costs are subtracted from income
a separate account in a school budget kept for one purpose, such as transportation
a yearly report of finances each Illinois school district must publish
a fixed extra payment for a job, such as coaching a team

look.title: Two Ways to Count
look.text: Count 1 subtracts only the cost of officials and ticket takers from the gate money. It shows a gain. Count 2 also subtracts police pay, electricity, buses, coaching stipends and field upkeep. It shows a loss. Both counts use real numbers from the same night.
look.prompt: Which count would you publish, and what would you tell the public about what it leaves out?

check.q: What is profit?
choices: the money left after costs are subtracted from income
a gift from a booster club
check.why: Profit is income minus costs, so the answer depends on which costs are counted.

check.q: Why can one game's costs be hard to find in a district budget?
choices: All costs are paid by the IHSA
Costs are split among separate funds and accounts
Ticket money goes to the federal government
check.why: Districts keep separate funds, so lights, buses and gate money may sit in different places.

check.q: Which yearly report must each Illinois district publish about its finances?
check.why: Illinois school law requires each district to publish a yearly Statement of Affairs.

lessons.title: A Budget on Display
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois law requires a school district to put its tentative budget on public display for thirty days and to hold a hearing before the board adopts it.
reading: Illinois public school districts run on a *fiscal year*, the twelve-month budget year, from July 1 to June 30. Each year the board must adopt a budget. The budget lists expected income and spending in each fund, including money for athletics. It is one of the most important votes a board takes.

State school law sets the steps. The board first prepares a *tentative budget*, a draft. The draft must be available for public inspection for at least thirty days before the board takes final action. The board must also hold a *public hearing* on the budget, with notice published in advance. Anyone can read the draft and speak at the hearing.

A second law covers taxes. Under the Illinois Truth in Taxation Law, a district that plans to raise its property tax levy by more than five percent over the year before must publish a notice and hold a hearing. For a parent asking what athletics cost, these steps are the moments when the numbers are on the table.

words.d: a twelve-month budget year; for Illinois school districts, July 1 to June 30
a draft budget shown to the public before a board adopts the final one
a meeting where members of the public may speak on a proposal before a vote
the amount of property tax a district asks to collect

look.title: Reading a Tentative Budget
look.text: A tentative budget is posted in the district office and online in late summer. The athletics line in the education fund shows coaching stipends and officials. Buses for away games appear in the transportation fund. Field lights appear in operations and maintenance. The hearing is set for thirty days later.
look.prompt: Before the hearing, what three lines would you add together to estimate the cost of the football season, and what would still be missing?

check.q: How long must an Illinois district's tentative budget be available to the public before final action?
check.why: State school law requires at least thirty days of public inspection before the board adopts the budget.

check.q: What is a fiscal year for an Illinois school district?
check.why: Illinois school districts use a fiscal year from July 1 to June 30.

check.q: When does the Truth in Taxation Law require a notice and hearing?
choices: when a team wins a state title
when a district plans to raise its levy by more than five percent
when a booster club gives a gift
check.why: A levy increase above five percent over the prior year triggers a published notice and a hearing.

lessons.title: A Stadium on the Ballot
lessons.mainIdea: Big high school stadium projects often go to a public vote, which turns a school's sports spending into an election question.
reading: Many school districts pay for large buildings with borrowed money that must be repaid from local taxes. In Illinois and many other states, voters must approve some of that borrowing at a *referendum*, a public vote on a single question. The question appears on a *ballot*, the list of choices voters mark. A new stadium can become one line on that ballot, beside new classrooms or roofs.

The largest high school stadiums are well known. In 2012 Allen High School in Texas opened a stadium that cost about $60 million. Voters in the district had approved the bonds that paid for it. News stories across the country compared its cost with that of college stadiums. Other Texas districts later built stadiums of similar size.

Such projects sharpen the old argument over civic ritual and revenue. Supporters said a stadium served the whole town as a civic space for graduations, band shows and games. Opponents said the money could have gone to classrooms. A referendum put that argument to the voters, who own the building through their district.

words.d: a public vote on a single question, such as whether a district may borrow to build
the list of choices voters mark in an election
a public place a community uses for shared events

look.title: Two Letters to the Editor
look.text: Letter 1: The stadium is where our town gathers. Graduation, the band festival and Friday games all happen there. It belongs to everyone. Letter 2: The same money could hire teachers and fix roofs for decades. A game lasts three hours. A classroom is used every day.
look.prompt: Which letter treats the stadium as a civic ritual space, and which treats it as a cost? What fact could each writer add from public records?

check.q: What is a referendum?
choices: a public vote on a single question
check.why: A referendum is a public vote on one question, such as approving school bonds.

check.q: About how much did Allen High School's stadium in Texas cost when it opened in 2012?
check.why: The Allen stadium, paid for with voter-approved bonds, cost about $60 million.

check.q: What is a civic space?
choices: a private box for team owners
a public place a community uses for shared events
a locker room for one team
check.why: Supporters called the stadium a civic space for graduations, band shows and games.

review.q: Why did adults take control of high school sport in the late 1800s and early 1900s?
choices: Ringers, age problems and loose money handling worried school leaders
review.why: Ringers, overage players and gate money run by students pushed educators to take charge.

review.q: Which statement about Chief Illiniwek is true?
choices: It began as a 1926 halftime performance and ended in 2007
It was created by the NCAA in 2005
It was a Texas high school mascot
It was protected by the Supreme Court in 2000
review.why: The figure first appeared at a University of Illinois halftime in 1926; the last official performance was in 2007.

review.q: What did Brentwood Academy (2001) mean for state athletic associations?
choices: Their actions can count as government action
review.why: The Court held the Tennessee association was a state actor, bound by constitutional limits.

review.q: Which pair of cases ruled against prayers sponsored by public schools?
choices: Brentwood Academy and Murphy v. NCAA
Flood v. Kuhn and NCAA v. Alston
Lee v. Weisman (1992) and Santa Fe v. Doe (2000)
Federal Baseball Club and Brentwood Academy
review.why: Lee struck down a clergy-led graduation prayer, and Santa Fe struck down a school-sponsored pregame prayer.

review.q: Which law lets a parent request a district's athletic invoices?
choices: the Illinois Freedom of Information Act
review.why: The Illinois FOIA, passed in 1984 and rewritten in 2010, lets anyone request public records.

review.q: Why can two honest people report different profits for the same game?
choices: One of them must be lying
They count different costs from different budget funds
review.why: Game costs sit in separate funds, so the result depends on which costs are included.

review.q: How does Title IX affect booster-funded gear for one team?
choices: It does not apply to boosters at all
The school must still provide equal treatment overall
review.why: The Office for Civil Rights looks at benefits athletes receive, whatever their source.

review.q: How long must an Illinois district's tentative budget be open to the public before the board adopts it?
review.why: The Illinois School Code requires at least thirty days of public inspection and a public hearing.
